# Affinity Mapping: How to Synthesize User Research Data in 5 Steps

Learn how to use this simple analysis method to uncover patterns and relationships in your UX data.

Sina Schreiber

\-

UX Researcher and Content Strategist at Condens

Last Updated:

January 4, 2025

Summary

[Qualitative UX research](https://www.userinterviews.com/blog/qualitative-research-sample-sizes) data from user interviews, usability studies, incoming user feedback, and other sources usually consist of a lot of notes, recordings, transcripts, and other unstructured information.

But how do you make sense of what you’ve gathered? Better still, maximizing the richness of these data but without missing deadlines?

**Affinity mapping** is one way to approach the synthesis of qualitative data.
In this article, we’ll cover the basics of affinity mapping and you’ll learn 5 concrete steps to conduct affinity mapping successfully.

## What is affinity mapping?

Affinity mapping—or affinity diagramming—is a synthesis technique in which you thematically analyze the data from qualitative research and organize everything in a way that allows you to better understand the information.

In other words, affinity mapping in UX research describes **the process of categorizing and sorting all qualitative research data based on similarities (or ‘affinities’)** . The output is an affinity diagram, a visually sorted and labeled wall of research data, which is why this method is sometimes also called affinity diagramming. It’s a common technique for [user research analysis](https://www.userinterviews.com/ux-research-field-guide-chapter/research-analysis) .

...

Affinity mapping is an excellent way to collaborate with your team and helps bring everyone closer to the user. But how do you manage this technique with a team?

A practical approach for [affinity mapping as a team](https://condens.io/freeletics) is to start by collectively assigning themes for the first session, then splitting up and continuing in smaller groups and coming back together to build clusters jointly. Make sure to set a leader for this task to help the team through this process.

[Inviting stakeholders in the research process](https://condens.io/blog/involving-stakeholders-in-ux-user-research) for affinity mapping can be a valuable way to engage them in user research findings, build a collective understanding of user research and open the doors for discussion around what you’ve found.

the backs of five people looking at a large poster with index cards

...

You can use spreadsheets or dedicated user research tools like [Condens](https://condens.io/) for tagging interesting research highlights.

###### Learn more about ["coding" qualitative research data](https://www.userinterviews.com/blog/qualitative-coding-ux-research-analysis) .

### Step 2: Create clusters.

After organizing all observations, statements, and highlights on notes, you can now start to build clusters to dive one level deeper into the research data. When you’ve assigned themes to your research data, you can start with one theme and then move through the other themes.

Get started by **picking the first note and creating the first cluster with it** , meaning, you place it on your (digital) wall where the affinity mapping will happen. **Pick the next one and check if it is related to the first note** and if you find a relevant commonality. Then, either group them or open a new cluster with the note.
There’s no right or wrong with what you define as the commonality of the group. However, it’s always a good idea to start by grouping commonalities around the topic of your research questions.

Pay attention to **emerging themes** and the need to split up grouped clusters to discover patterns in your research data. Then, whenever you find something, document this pattern and **name the clusters to keep track of what you’ve found so far** . Go through the entire stack following this approach.

💡Tip: At the end of affinity mapping, you can also turn the cluster names into short summaries of what you’ve learned with that cluster which can be shared as a key insight with the team.

‍

An example of a physical affinity map (a poster with sticky notes)

_Example of affinity mapping on a poster for a recent UX research study on mental health apps and habit tracking._

### Step 3: Repeat the process.

...

### Step 5: Zoom out and analyze the relationship between clusters.

When having a (digital) wall full of clusters around affinities in the research data, try to look at the picture further away. It’s a good idea to **zoom out at the end of the process to see how the different clusters relate to each other** and allow cross-cluster analysis.

You can think of this step as further sorting, but now with whole clusters to see which are more important to others and which have dependencies or order. Don’t hesitate to segment the clusters or draw connections between coherent clusters.

## Wrap up

Affinity mapping helps you to categorize and sort qualitative UX research data, find patterns in the gathered information and draw conclusions.

As the last step for successful affinity mapping, it’s crucial to convert the findings into output.

### **What are codes and tags?**

Codes and tags are the building blocks of qualitative data analysis in UX research synthesis. They're labels you use to categorize your data, making it easier to organize and analyze.

There are different types of tags and coding practices, including:

* Descriptive codes: Summarize the topic of a piece of data (e.g., "navigation", "error message")
* Process codes: Capture actions (e.g., "workaround", "abandoning task")
* Emotion codes: Describe feelings or experiences (e.g., "frustration", "confusion")

The goal is to create a system that helps you make sense of your data and uncover meaningful insights.

## What is affinity diagramming?

Affinity diagramming is a popular UX research synthesis method. It involves grouping related pieces of information together to identify themes and patterns. Here's how it works:

1. Write each piece of data on a sticky note
2. Place similar notes together in groups
3. Label each group with a theme or insight
4. Look for connections between groups

This method helps you visualize your data and spot patterns more easily.

> [Here’s a detailed guide to affinity mapping, and the tools that can help you do it.](https://www.looppanel.com/blog/affinity-mapping-guide)

### **How do I know something is a pattern or trend?**

Identifying patterns is key in UX research synthesis. Look for:

* **Repetition:** Does this issue or behavior show up multiple times?
* **Consistency:** Is this theme present across different user types or scenarios?
* **Impact:** How significant is this issue for users?

Remember, a pattern doesn't always mean majority. Sometimes, an insight from a minority of users can be just as valuable.

### **How to synthesize data, analyze it, and gain insights**

1. **Organize your data:** Use your codes and tags to categorize information
2. **Look for patterns:** Use methods like affinity diagramming to group related data
3. **Ask questions:** What does this pattern mean? Why might users be behaving this way?
4. **Generate insights:** What does this tell us about our users' needs or problems?
5. **Validate:** Check your insights against your raw data to ensure they're supported

## **Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)**

#### **What is the difference between** [**analysis**](https://www.looppanel.com/blog/how-to-run-ux-research-analysis) **and synthesis in UX research?**

In UX research, analysis and synthesis are two sides of the same coin, both crucial in the user research synthesis process. Analysis is about breaking down data into smaller parts, examining each piece in detail. It's the first step in making sense of your research findings.
Synthesis, on the other hand, is about putting these pieces back together to form a cohesive whole. It's where the magic of UX research synthesis happens.

While analysis helps you understand individual data points, synthesis in UX research is about connecting the dots. It's where you start to see patterns emerge and gain deeper insights into user behavior. For example, you might analyze individual user comments about a product feature, but through synthesis, you could uncover a broader trend about how users interact with your product. This synthesis stage is where many UX research synthesis methods come into play, helping researchers transform raw data into actionable insights.

#### **What are the methods of synthesizing research?**

There are numerous UX research synthesis methods available to researchers, each offering unique ways to make sense of data. Affinity diagramming is a popular technique where researchers group related pieces of information to identify themes.
This method is particularly useful when dealing with large amounts of qualitative data from user interviews or usability tests.

Another key approach in user research synthesis is journey mapping. This involves creating a visual representation of a user's experience over time, helping to identify pain points and opportunities. Thematic analysis, persona creation, and empathy mapping are also valuable UX research synthesis methods. Each of these techniques offers different ways to organize and interpret your data, allowing you to approach your research from multiple angles. The key is to choose the synthesis methods that best fit your research questions and the type of data you've collected. By mastering these various approaches to UX research synthesis, you can ensure that your research findings translate into meaningful improvements in user experience.

#### **What are valuable research insights?**

Valuable research insights are the ultimate goal of UX research synthesis.

...

When writing your synthesis, clearly state your main findings and support them with evidence from your research. Remember, synthesis in research is about connecting ideas and presenting a cohesive understanding of your topic. To effectively synthesize research, focus on the relationships between different pieces of information and how they contribute to answering your research questions.

#### **What is the synthesis format in research? / What is the format of synthesis?**

The synthesis format in research typically follows a structured approach. It usually begins with an introduction that outlines the research question and context. The main body of the synthesis presents key themes or findings, with each point supported by evidence from multiple sources. A good format for synthesis includes comparing and contrasting different perspectives on each theme. The conclusion of your synthesis should summarize the main points and offer insights or recommendations based on your analysis.
This format of synthesis helps to organize complex information into a clear, logical narrative that effectively communicates your research findings.

## **What is an Affinity Diagram?**

An affinity diagram is a tool often used to organize data and ideas. Affinity diagrams help you organize information into groups of similar items to then analyze qualitative data or observations.

Business and design teams have used affinity diagrams for a long time to organize ideas, complex information and even customer feedback into themes or groups. For UX researchers, affinity diagrams are often used for analyzing and synthesizing user research findings by patterns and themes. In this case affinity diagrams are sometimes referred to as the KJ method or an affinity map.

...

Doing thematic analysis using an affinity diagram helps you find patterns, create themes and figure out what you learned from qualitative research by quickly grouping data and finding connections between those groups quickly and effectively.

### **Affinity Diagrams for User Research Analysis & Synthesis**

Using an affinity diagram can help you analyze and synthesize user research findings. The most common method of analyzing user research is thematic analysis. In thematic analysis, researchers aim to make sense of all the user research notes and observations they made by creating themes to further organize and explain what they learned. Naturally an affinity diagram is a tool generally used to create groups and themes from user research data since it is an effective way to categorize qualitative data!

Themes from user research are entirely dependent on your research and goals. Here are some examples and ideas for creating useful themes from your UX research data:
* Answers to specific research questions
* Frequently seen or heard topics/ideas
* Summary of related notes, observations and data

## **Steps to Creating and Affinity Diagram**

1. Record all notes or observations on individual cards or sticky notes
2. Look for patterns and notes or observations that are related
3. Create a group for each pattern or theme
4. Give each theme or group a name
5. Bonus: create a statement of what you learned about each group (this is often referred to as a Key Insight in UX research)

## **Examples of Affinity Diagrams and Thematic Analysis for UX Research**

# Affinity diagrams: How to turn UX data into design insights

> Affinity diagrams turn messy UX research into themes and insights. Collect, cluster, and label data to guide user-centered design decisions.

Oct 17, 2025

Authors

Ella Webber Writer

Sharan Phillora Writer

In this article

1. [01\. What are affinity diagrams?](https://maze.co/blog/affinity-diagrams/ "What are affinity diagrams?")
2. 02\. How to use affinity diagrams in UX research/design
3. 03\. How to create an affinity diagram in 6 steps
4. 04\. Affinity diagramming examples and scenarios
5. 05\. Our favorite affinity diagram templates

Share

#### TL;DR

Affinity diagrams, also called affinity maps, help UX teams turn messy qualitative data into organized insights.

Researchers collect raw data from interviews, surveys, or usability tests and place each point on a note. They move those notes onto a shared board, group related notes together, and give each cluster a clear theme.

...

** Affinity mapping is also known as the KJ method because it was first invented by a Japanese anthropologist named Jiro Kawakita. It’s now a part of the Seven Management and Planning Tools widely used in Japan.

## How to use affinity diagrams in UX research/design

Affinity mapping can be used for analyzing large volumes of qualitative data. This might come from [UX research methods](https://maze.co/guides/ux-research/ux-research-methods/) like [card sorting](https://maze.co/guides/card-sorting/) , customer feedback and [UX surveys](https://maze.co/guides/ux-surveys/) , or team brainstorming sessions.

[UX teams](https://maze.co/collections/ux-ui-design/ux-team-structure/) create affinity diagrams to document their ideas, observations, and research. Here are a few common use cases for affinity diagramming in UX:

* **Analyzing user research:** Affinity diagrams are widely used to make sense of the wealth of customer data from user interviews, field studies, and usability testing.

...

Importantly, affinity mapping was not the only tool she used. It was part of a larger workflow that included surveys, app store review analysis, personas, and usability testing. But the affinity map was the step that **synthesized qualitative findings into themes** , a bridge between raw research and the design ideas that followed, such as:

* A redesigned filter system with total price, radius, and tags
* Group list commenting to reduce the friction of coordinating bookings
* Experience carousels to nudge adoption through social proof

This case study shows how affinity diagrams slot into a broader UX research process: they don’t replace other methods, but they **turn scattered insights into patterns** that designers can build from.

While Sonia’s case study shows how affinity mapping works in practice, you don’t need to run a full redesign project to see its value.

results.title: Synthesising UX Research
excerpts:
Synthesis is the step that comes after the designer has understood the problem statement. Once the UX research is conducted and sufficient raw data is received, it is converted to valuable insights. It is the process of creating intuitive concepts based on the facts that are being analysed. When considering UX research, it typically means the conversion of themes and ideas into meaningful information.

Simply put, synthesis is a process wherein a researcher tries to make sense of the data collected using UX research. It works to create a model of reality that includes journey maps, personas, and affinity diagrams to help gain a better understanding of the problem statement at hand and use it in both internal as well as external communication.

### Importance of Synthesis in UX Research

Often, the importance of synthesis is undervalued, mostly because of short deadlines and tight budgets.
